turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Hey, sorry we're late, parking was a mess. Leo's six and we're here for these really itchy dry patches behind his knees and inside the elbows.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're fine. Leo, what's it feel like?
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): It itches so bad. Am I sick? Is it gonna spread?
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): It doesn't spread person to person, and you're not in trouble. Mom, when did this itching start?
[SEG0005] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Umm, I can't pin the exact day. About three weeks? Well, actually maybe right after his birthday, I really don't know.
[SEG0006] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Longer. I started weekdays before spring break and he was already scratching, so err, more like two months.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, roughly three weeks to two months, and no exact start date. Worse at a certain time?
[SEG0008] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Nights. He scratches till the sheets are, uh, wrecked.
[SEG0009] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He sleeps badly, up a lot. Daytime he's wiped out too, really tired, droopy on the couch.
[SEG0010] person_3 (PATIENT): No. I'm not tired. I played. I'm not.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright, he disagrees with you on the tiredness. Any fever?
[SEG0012] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No. No fever.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any wheeze or trouble breathing? I ask 'cause this can run with asthma in a family.
[SEG0014] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): His father has asthma, the inhaler kind. Leo doesn't wheeze. Breathing's been fine.
[SEG0015] person_3 (PATIENT): Am I gonna get asthma? Do I need a shot? Will it hurt?

[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): No shot today. Dad's asthma isn't automatically yours. I see dry scaly patches in both elbow creases and behind both knees, and scratch marks. No oozing, doesn't look infected.
[SEG0017] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He scraped his shin at the park. Looked like it healed okay to me.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any wounds that heal slowly?
[SEG0019] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No. That scrape closed in five days. Normal.
[SEG0020] person_3 (PATIENT): Is five days good? You gonna put cream on me?
[SEG0021] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We've been using the white cream on the patches twice a day. It's the hydrocortisone, one percent, I'm pretty sure.
[SEG0022] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Hydrocortazone, right, thin layer morning and night. I go with whatever's on the box.

[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): The nurse read that tube in the hall a minute ago and she said two point five percent, not the one percent. Those don't match, so I won't lock in a dose. We'll set the white tube aside. What do you moisturize with?
[SEG0024] person_4 (CAREGIVER): The big blue tub. Label's gone, I can't tell you the name. He fights it and I skip Sundays.
[SEG0025] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Saturdays, not Sundays. Soccer. That's the day we miss the blue stuff.
[SEG0026] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah, soccer day. Not Sunday. Sunday's pancakes.
[SEG0027] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Saturdays, my mistake. My sister's little girl gets dry skin and she slathers coconut oil on her, but that's her kid, not something I'm deciding here.

[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Your sister's coconut oil stays out of Leo's plan. The way this works, the skin barrier isn't holding water in, so the skin dries, the itch nerves fire, and scratching cracks the barrier further. My working impression is eczema, atopic dermatitis, provisional not lab-confirmed, from the creases, the night itch, his dad's asthma, and the exam.
[SEG0029] person_3 (PATIENT): Is eczema forever? Can I still play soccer? Will the new cream sting?

[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Lots of kids keep playing, it flares and settles. I'm starting triamcinolone, point one percent cream, a thin layer on the patches only, twice a day for seven days, then stop. Keep it off his face. It can sting a second, usually not bad.
[SEG0031] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Twice a day for seven days, okay. Do we keep the blue tub?

[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Stop the blue tub since nobody can name it, and don't go back to that white steroid. Use plain petrolatum, Vaseline, a thick coat on the dry skin at least four times a day, always right after a short lukewarm bath. Pat dry, don't rub.
[SEG0033] person_3 (PATIENT): Four times? It'll be sticky. Do I have to? What if I hate it?
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sticky is okay, and yes, that coat is what protects the skin. Any allergies to medicines or creams?
[SEG0035] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No. None that we know of.
[SEG0036] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Sorry, I'll mute this. Go ahead.

[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thanks. Temperature right now is ninety eight point six fahrenheit and his pulse is 92. Let me mirror the story so we're aligned. Itchy dry patches at the elbows and behind the knees, roughly three weeks to two months with no exact start, worse at night, sleep broken, daytime tiredness not agreed, father with asthma, no fever, no wheeze, no allergies, the shin scrape healed in five days, the steroid strength doesn't match, and the blue tub has no name and gets skipped on Saturdays.
[SEG0038] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yeah, that's the shape of it. What if the skin gets oozy or infected?
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): If it oozes, the redness spreads, or he gets a fever, call the office. Otherwise I'll see him back in two weeks, just to look.
[SEG0040] person_3 (PATIENT): Two weeks? You promise it won't hurt? Can I still play soccer?
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): Promise, nothing we do today hurts, and soccer is okay. We'll check the patches in two weeks.

spec.situation: Mother brings a child with itchy dry patches behind the knees and elbows, worse at night, scratching; creams named by colour; father has asthma; doctor adjusts steroid cream and moisturiser advice.

traps.happens: The doctor (or nurse) explains a mechanism or a diagnosis in the patient's body ('the voice box is irritated by reflux', 'diabetes dulls the nerves in the feet', 'the swelling is your body fighting infection'). A nurse or caregiver also mentions a fact about THEIR OWN life (their sister, their child, their own illness).
traps.label_rule: Explanations by the doctor are NEVER symptoms, history or social history of the patient; they may only appear as clinical_assessment or counselling if the doctor stated them as such. A nurse's or caregiver's own life facts are not recorded as the patient's. Each symptom's reported_by is the person who really described it.

traps.happens: A caregiver or relative reports observations ('the cut healed in five days', 'she sleeps badly', 'he does not take the tablets on Sundays'); the patient agrees, disagrees or corrects one point. The nurse also reports a measurement that the patient mentioned before.
traps.label_rule: reported_by follows who said it. A healing cut that healed normally is a negative finding (no slow-healing wounds) or nothing, NOT a symptom. A disputed fact is recorded with certainty disputed or as an uncertainty. A correction replaces the earlier value (Saturday, not Sunday).

features: spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.
disputed_numbers: the nurse reads a value and the patient or relative disagrees or remembers another (a dose, a weight, a BP). Keep both and record an uncertainty.

bad.reason: Stopped white steroid is supported, but hydrocortisone identity is uncertain and reported by family member, not doctor.

bad.text: unlabeled blue tub cream (indication=moisturizing, status=discontinued, reported_by=caregiver)

bad.reason: Scratch marks are present, but transcript doesn't localize them specifically to both elbow creases and popliteal fossae.
bad.text: Scratch marks (body_site=bilateral elbow creases and popliteal fossae, status=present, observed_by=doctor)

omissions.text: Hydrocortisone strength is not confirmed and should not be locked in as hydrocortisone 1%; family member said 1% but the nurse read the tube as 2.5%.
Triamcinolone 0.1% cream should be applied as a thin layer on the patches only.
Petrolatum/Vaseline should be used as a thick coat.
Petrolatum/Vaseline should be applied always right after a short lukewarm bath, and the skin should be patted dry rather than rubbed.
No trouble breathing was specifically asked about and denied along with no wheeze.
Exam finding: no oozing of the rash.
Follow-up warning signs included skin oozing, spreading redness, or fever; spreading redness is missing.

omissions.text: Prior white steroid use was described as a thin layer morning and night/twice a day; the recorded medication entry for hydrocortisone is missing the application amount/instructions and the strength is not locked in because family said 1% but nurse read 2.5%.
Doctor specifically advised triamcinolone 0.1% cream to be applied as a thin layer on the patches only, and then stop after seven days; 'patches only' is not captured in the medication entry.
Doctor advised to keep triamcinolone off the face; this site restriction is not captured in the medication entry.
Petrolatum was specified as plain petrolatum/Vaseline and to apply a thick coat on the dry skin; the medication entry does not capture 'plain' or 'thick coat on dry skin'.

There was a disagreement about which day the moisturizer was skipped: caregiver first said Sundays, then family member/patient corrected this to Saturdays; the discrepancy itself is not recorded, only the final Saturday schedule.
Exam finding was that the dry scaly patches and scratch marks were bilateral: both elbow creases and behind both knees. Scratch marks entry lacks body site detail.

The child had a shin scrape at the park that healed normally/closed in five days; only the negative finding of slow-healing wounds is recorded, not the supporting history of the recent scrape healing okay.

Return precautions included spreading redness as a warning sign of possible infection/flare needing a call; this is recorded, but the family specifically asked about 'oozy or infected' skin, showing concern about infection, which is not captured as part of the discussion context.
